Every single kopeck of ours was there.
The money was for our second floor.
And for new furniture for the restaurant.
I do not even have anything to pay salaries with now.

I might as well sell our restaurant now.

See you!

meanings.note: Financial institution. Common masculine noun meaning 'bank' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: У неё есть счёт в банке.
examples.trans: She has a bank account.
The bank closes at six o'clock.

examples.text: Или счёт в банке. Потому что они все обманщики.
examples.trans: Or a bank account. Because they are all cheats.

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'jar'.

examples.trans: The supplier will bring the jar in an hour.
Hide the jar under the table!

examples.text: Шеф ничего не узнает, прячь банку!
examples.trans: Chef will not find out anything, hide the jar!

meanings.note: Land along the edge of water. Common masculine noun meaning 'shore, bank' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: They will sit quietly on the shore.
They walked along the lake shore.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'guard / keep safe'.

examples.text: Вот последняя банка, на, береги её.
examples.trans: Here is the last jar, take it and guard it.
Keep this last jar safe.

examples.text: Потом заправились и спокойно дошли к берегу.
examples.trans: Then we refueled and calmly reached the shore.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Present есть; у меня есть = I have. Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: The neuter form 'всё' used alone. Core Russian det meaning 'all, whole; everyone, everything' in everyday speech.
Neuter всё. Core Russian det meaning 'all, whole; everyone, everything' in everyday speech.
Plural все. Core Russian det meaning 'all, whole; everyone, everything' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
As you all know...
Share with everyone.

meanings.note: Pointing at something. Core Russian part meaning 'here, there (pointing)' in everyday speech.
Emphasis. Core Russian part meaning 'here, there (pointing)' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: There, look.
Here's my toy car.
All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: Ordinal number. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('second').

examples.trans: This is my second term.
The second lesson is hard.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people

meanings.en: other forms: вас (gen/acc), вам (dat), вами (instr), вас (prep)
meanings.note: Case forms. Core Russian pron meaning 'you (polite or plural)' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: As you all know...
Does the governor support you?

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: В гости = for a visit. Abstract feminine noun formed with the Slavic suffix '-ость' ('-ness, -ity') from the corresponding adjective. Common masculine noun meaning 'guest, visitor' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: You have visitors!
We're going visiting.

examples.text: Клавдия Викторовна, к вам гости! Па-пам!
examples.trans: Klavdia Viktorovna, you have visitors! Ta-da!

meanings.note: давай + 1st person plural or infinitive
давай + 1st person plural or infinitive

examples.trans: Let's talk.
He gives me a book.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: Core Russian part meaning 'even' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Even a child knows.
Even Mum doesn't know.
Yes! Even a child knows.

meanings.note: plural only: there is no singular in everyday use

examples.trans: I have no money.
The money is on the table.
Gum? I didn't have enough money.

meanings.note: + genitive. Core Russian prep meaning 'for' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.
This is for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: Singular only. Common feminine noun meaning 'food, meal' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Oh, bad food?

examples.text: В этом ресторане всегда свежая еда.
examples.trans: There is always fresh food in this restaurant.
Oh no, bad food? Does your stomach hurt?

ехать.gloss: to go (by vehicle), to drive, to ride

meanings.en: to go, to drive, to ride
meanings.note: by car, bus, train, in one direction, now
'едем' = we're going / let's go. Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to go (by vehicle), to drive, to ride', paired with 'поехать'.

examples.trans: Vitalik, we're going to the Santa Fe.
Let's go!

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'купать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to purchase / stock up'.

examples.text: Мне теперь еду закупать не на что.
examples.trans: I have nothing to buy food with now.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и закупать вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and to purchase on time.

meanings.note: жить на зарплату = to live on one's salary

examples.trans: He lives on his salary.
He has a good salary.

examples.text: Эдуард Владимирович учёный, и он живёт на зарплату.
examples.trans: Eduard Vladimirovich is a scholar, and he lives on a salary.

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: + genitive: 'из мэрии' = from the town hall

examples.trans: The town hall called me.
He's from Moscow.

examples.text: Марина Сергеевна, я уже знаю. Мне звонили из мэрии.
examples.trans: Marina Sergeyevna, I already know. The town hall called me.

meanings.note: + dative. Core Russian prep meaning 'to, towards' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.
I'm going to Mum's.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Каждый день = every day. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('every, each').

examples.trans: Every day.
Every person.

examples.text: Аркаш, мне москвичи звонят каждый день. Может, всё-таки передумаем?
examples.trans: Arkasha, the people from Moscow call me every day. Maybe we should reconsider after all?

meanings.note: Question word. Core Russian adv meaning 'how; as' in everyday speech.
Как вы знаете = as you know. Core Russian adv meaning 'how; as' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: How was it in Hungary?
As you all know...
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.en: kopeck, one hundredth of a rouble
meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'kopeck' in everyday Russian.
Common feminine noun meaning 'kopeck' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I haven't got a penny.
It costs next to nothing.

examples.text: Пятьсот. А у меня ни копейки.
examples.trans: Five hundred. And I haven't got a penny.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'kites / vultures' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: They have flocked here like vultures.

examples.text: На кухне ресторана всегда есть коршун.
examples.trans: In the restaurant kitchen there is always kites.

meanings.note: Uncountable, singular only. Common feminine noun meaning 'furniture' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: With furniture?
The furniture is new.
Of course, with furniture.

meanings.note: Agrees with the thing owned. Core Russian det meaning 'my, mine' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Where's my toy car?
That's mine.
No. That's mine.

meanings.note: + prepositional: на сайте. Core Russian prep meaning 'on, onto; for' in everyday speech.
+ accusative: на второй срок. Core Russian prep meaning 'on, onto; for' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.trans: I love our town.
This is our flat.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

examples.trans: I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'nothing (to do it with)', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Конечно, нашему ресторану нужен хороший хозяин.
examples.trans: Of course, our restaurant needs a good owner.

examples.text: Мне даже зарплату теперь платить нечем.
examples.trans: I do not even have anything to pay salaries with now.

examples.text: Нам гостей в зале кормить совсем нечем.
examples.trans: We have nothing at all to feed the guests in the hall.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('new').

examples.trans: A new house.
I need a new job.

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to her', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Она нашла нас на новом месте.
examples.trans: She found us at the new place.
That is it, she got really offended.
She is not answering her phone.

meanings.note: Core Russian pron meaning 'they' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: They are building a centre.
History will punish them.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: Often with annoyance. Core Russian adv meaning 'again' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: It's another trick.
Rain again.

examples.text: Нина, не слушай. Это опять обман.
examples.trans: Nina, don't listen. It's another trick.

meanings.note: платить за + accusative = to pay for

examples.trans: We pay well.
Who is paying?

examples.text: А вашу работу вернуть можно. И мы хорошо платим.
examples.trans: But we can get your job back for you. And we pay well.

meanings.note: понимаешь? = you know? do you understand?

examples.trans: I understand.
I want to go to the sea, you know?

examples.text: Я хочу нормально жить! Я хочу биде, понимаешь?
examples.trans: I want to live like a normal person! I want a bidet, do you understand?

meanings.note: Последний раз = for the last time. Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'следний'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('last, final').

examples.trans: I'm asking for the last time.
This is our last chance.
I'm asking for the last time. Where is the money?

meanings.note: On foot, once. Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to come, to arrive', paired with 'приходить'.

examples.trans: Security will be here any moment.
I'll come tomorrow.

examples.text: Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
examples.trans: Don't, Samson. Security will be here any second.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'давать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to sell'.

examples.trans: How much are you selling them for?

examples.text: Конечно надо! Почём ты их продаёшь?
examples.trans: Of course I do! How much are you selling them for?
So you really are selling it?

meanings.en: to relax, let one's guard down
meanings.note: Reflexive imperfective verb. Prefix 'рас-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'слабляться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to relax', paired with 'расслабиться'.

examples.trans: We cannot let our guard down now.

examples.text: Он любит расслабляться под хорошую музыку.
examples.trans: He likes to relax to good music.

examples.text: Тогда работай усердно и не расслабляйся.
examples.trans: Then work hard and do not relax.

meanings.note: informal: a group of young men; ребята! = guys!
Colloquial plural of ребёнок. Common substantive noun meaning 'guys, lads, kids (plural only)' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Guys, where are you?
The boys will have a word with you.

examples.text: Тогда ребята с тобой поработают. До свидания, Аркадий Борисович.
examples.trans: Then the boys will have a little word with you. Goodbye, Arkady Borisovich.

meanings.note: Dining establishment. Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.trans: They called from the Italian restaurant.
In the evening they went to a restaurant.

examples.text: Кстати, звонили из итальянского ресторана. Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: By the way, they called from the Italian restaurant. They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: I'm in the office now.
I'll be right there.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'net, network' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Quickly get all the nets!

examples.text: Рыбаки на рассвете быстро вытащили полные сети на берег.
examples.trans: At dawn the fishermen quickly hauled the full nets onto the shore.

examples.text: Крупная ресторанная сеть хотела перекупить нашего лучшего шефа.
examples.trans: A large restaurant chain wanted to poach our best chef.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лететься'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'flocked together'.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и слететься вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and flocked together on time.

examples.text: На нашей кухне все умеют слететься.
examples.trans: In our kitchen everyone knows how to flocked together.

meanings.note: Direction. Core Russian adv meaning 'here (to this place)' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Give me the keys.
Come here!
The white one? Give me the keys.

meanings.note: там такие деньги = there's so much money in it

examples.trans: Everything's fine there.
Who's there?
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: As opposed to before. Core Russian adv meaning 'now (from now on)' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Now I'm the boss.
Now everything's fine.

examples.text: Теперь я начальник нашей стройки. Ты уволен!
examples.trans: Now I'm the boss of our building site. You're fired!

увидеться.gloss: to see each other, meet up

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'видеться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to see each other, meet up', paired with 'видеться'.

examples.text: Послушай, мы сегодня увидимся вечером с тобой?
examples.trans: Listen, will we see each other this evening?
See you tomorrow!
All right, see you in the kitchen, administrator!

meanings.note: Дай хоть одну = give me just one. Core Russian part meaning 'at least, just' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: Give me just one.
At least a little.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: the plural is a different word: люди, людям, о людях
Plural люди, a different word. Common masculine noun meaning 'person; (pl) people' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He is a good person.
There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: Question word. Core Russian pron meaning 'what' in everyday speech.
Conjunction. Core Russian pron meaning 'what' in everyday speech.
Core Russian pron meaning 'what' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: Of a building. Common masculine noun meaning 'floor, storey' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: У нас ведь второй этаж, да?
examples.trans: Ours is the second floor, right?
They live on the third floor.

examples.text: У нас ведь второй этаж, да? Давай, слушаем.
examples.trans: Ours is the second floor, right? Go on, let's listen.

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)

meanings.en: other forms: меня (gen/acc), мне (dat), мной (instr), мне (prep)
meanings.note: Case forms. Core Russian pron meaning 'I' in everyday speech.

examples.trans: I'm doing my homework.
I grew up here.
Chef, I didn't take it.
